title: LFU Cache
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning for the eviction candidate versus frequency buckets ordered by recency.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a Least Frequently Used (LFU) cache with a fixed capacity, supporting get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1) time. When the cache is full and a new key needs to be inserted, evict the key with the smallest use frequency; if multiple keys share that smallest frequency, evict whichever of them was used least recently.

blocks.caption: Keys are grouped by frequency, and each frequency group keeps its own recency order for tie-breaking

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Design a Least Frequently Used (LFU) cache with a fixed capacity, supporting get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1) time. When the cache is full and a new key needs to be inserted, evict the key with the smallest use frequency; if multiple keys share that smallest frequency, evict whichever of them was used least recently.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Small Fridge That Keeps the Most Popular Snacks
blocks.text: Like a small dorm fridge with limited shelf space, where whenever a new snack needs to go in and there is no room left, whichever snack has been grabbed the fewest times gets thrown out first, and if there is a tie in popularity, the one that has been sitting untouched the longest goes.

blocks.caption: Track how often and how recently each key is used, evicting the least frequently (then least recently) used

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: capacity 2, put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Result","Why"],"rows":[["put(1, 1)","cache: {1:1}, frequency of 1 is now 1","A brand new key always starts at frequency 1, its very first use"],["put(2, 2)","cache: {1:1, 2:2}, both at frequency 1","Key 2 is also brand new, joining key 1 in the frequency-1 group"],["get(1)","returns 1, frequency of 1 becomes 2","Reading key 1 counts as a use, bumping its frequency from 1 to 2 and moving it out of the frequency-1 group"],["put(3, 3)","cache is full, key 2 has the lowest frequency (1), so it is evicted; cache becomes {1:1, 3:3}","With key 1 now at frequency 2, key 2 is the sole occupant of the frequency-1 group, the current minimum, making it the eviction target"]]}

blocks.text: Example: continuing, get(2), get(3), put(4,4)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Result","Why"],"rows":[["get(2)","-1, since key 2 was already evicted","Key 2 no longer exists in the cache, so it cannot be found"],["get(3)","3, frequency of 3 becomes 2","Reading key 3 counts as a use, raising its frequency from 1 to 2"],["put(4, 4)","cache is full again, keys 1 and 3 are tied at frequency 2, but 1 was used less recently, so 1 is evicted","Both remaining keys share the same frequency, so the tie is broken by recency, and key 1's most recent use happened before key 3's just-performed get"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: capacity 0
With a capacity of 0, the cache can never hold any key at all, so every put call is effectively ignored and every get call returns -1.
5. How Should We Think?

Before designing anything, notice this problem asks for the same kind of thing All O`one Data Structure needed, instant access to an extreme by a changing count, but now with an extra twist: ties at that extreme must be broken by recency, not left arbitrary.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The eviction rule has two levels: first find the smallest frequency currently present, then, among keys at that frequency, find the least recently used one; both parts must be answered in O(1).

Observation 2: Just like All O`one Data Structure, grouping keys by their current frequency into separate buckets, with a running minFreq pointer, answers the first part directly: the minFreq bucket always holds exactly the lowest-frequency keys.

Observation 3: Within a single frequency bucket, "least recently used" is exactly what an insertion-ordered structure, such as an ordered dictionary, a linked hash set, or a doubly linked list, naturally tracks: the oldest entry sits at one end, ready to be evicted, and any key can be moved to the "most recent" end in O(1) when it is used again.

Observation 4: Since a get or a successful put always increases a key's frequency by exactly 1, the key simply moves from its current frequency bucket to the next one up, always landing as the most recently used entry there, since it was just used; if its old bucket was the minFreq bucket and is now empty, minFreq moves up by exactly 1.

Whenever an eviction or extraction rule has two levels, a primary changing quantity to bucket by, and a secondary tie-break to order within each bucket, combine a bucket-by-primary-key structure with a recency-ordered structure inside each bucket.

This is the direct extension of All O`one Data Structure: swap that problem's plain set of keys per bucket for an insertion-ordered set per bucket, and the exact same bucket-and-pointer machinery now also handles the recency tie-break for free.
6. Brute Force Solution

Store every key alongside its value, its usage frequency, and the last time it was used. On eviction, scan the entire cache to find the key with the lowest frequency, breaking ties by the oldest last-used time.
Step by step algorithm

items: Keep a hash map from key to (value, frequency, last used time).
get and put update the frequency and last used time directly for O(1) access.
On eviction, scan every entry in the cache to find the one with the lowest frequency, breaking ties by the least recently used time.

codes.python:
class LFUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.cache = {}                                          # key to [value, frequency, last_used_time]
        self.clock = 0

    def _touch(self, key):
        self.clock += 1
        self.cache[key][1] += 1
        self.cache[key][2] = self.clock

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        self._touch(key)
        return self.cache[key][0]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.capacity == 0:
            return
        if key in self.cache:
            self.cache[key][0] = value
            self._touch(key)
            return
        if len(self.cache) >= self.capacity:
            evict_key = min(self.cache, key=lambda k: (self.cache[k][1], self.cache[k][2]))  # scans everything
            del self.cache[evict_key]
        self.clock += 1
        self.cache[key] = [value, 1, self.clock]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cache = LFUCache(2)
    cache.put(1, 1)
    cache.put(2, 2)
    print(cache.get(1))
    cache.put(3, 3)
    print(cache.get(2))
    print(cache.get(3))
    cache.put(4, 4)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Each cache entry stores value, frequency, and a last-used timestamp together, since eviction needs all three pieces of information simultaneously to make its two-level decision.
_touch centralizes the "this key was just used" logic, bumping frequency and stamping the current clock value, so both get and a put on an existing key share the exact same update behavior.
Eviction compares by frequency first and last-used time second in one combined key, naturally implementing "smallest frequency first, ties broken by the oldest timestamp" in a single expression.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
get and put correctly maintain frequency and recency, and eviction correctly identifies the least frequently, then least recently, used key.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for get and put in the common case, but O(capacity) whenever eviction is needed, due to the full scan.
Space: O(capacity), for the cache entries.
Limitation: the problem requires every operation, including eviction, to run in true O(1), which a full scan can never provide.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's eviction cost comes entirely from re-deriving, by scanning everything, information that barely changes between operations: only one key's frequency and timestamp actually shift on any given call, yet the scan re-examines every key's frequency and timestamp regardless. The fix mirrors All O`one Data Structure directly: instead of storing frequency as just a number to be compared against every other number, use it as a bucket label, grouping keys that currently share a frequency together. The remaining piece unique to this problem is that a bucket itself needs internal order, since a tie in frequency must still be resolved by recency, so each bucket becomes a small recency-ordered structure, evict from one end, promote to the other, instead of a plain unordered set. With buckets tracked by a hash map and a running minFreq pointer, both frequency comparison and recency tie-breaking collapse to O(1) structural operations, no scanning required for either.

Group keys by their current frequency, using a hash map from frequency to an ordered structure, such as an insertion ordered set or list, of keys currently at that exact frequency, ordered from least to most recently used within the group. Maintain a running minFreq pointer tracking the smallest frequency currently present. On get or put for an existing key, remove it from its current frequency group, increment its frequency, and re-insert it as the most recently used entry of its new frequency group, updating minFreq if its old group becomes empty. On put for a brand new key, evict the least recently used key from the minFreq group if the cache is full, then insert the new key at frequency 1 and reset minFreq to 1.
9. Optimized Solution
A hash map of frequency to an insertion ordered group of keys, plus a running minFreq pointer, giving O(1) get, put, and eviction.
Dry run for capacity 2: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3)

items: put(1, 1): cache empty, insert key 1 at frequency 1. minFreq becomes 1, since this is the only key present and every key starts fresh at frequency 1.
put(2, 2): insert key 2 at frequency 1, alongside key 1, with key 2 recorded as the more recently added of the two within that same frequency-1 group.
get(1): key 1 moves from the frequency-1 group to the frequency-2 group, since reading it counts as a use; the frequency-1 group still has key 2 left in it, so minFreq correctly stays at 1.

put(3, 3): cache is full (2 keys), so evict the least recently used key from the minFreq (1) group, which is key 2, the older of the two entries ever placed there; insert key 3 at frequency 1, and minFreq resets to 1 since a fresh key always starts the minimum over again.

blocks.caption: Optimized: keys grouped by frequency, ordered by recency within each group, with a running minFreq pointer

codes.python:
from collections import OrderedDict, defaultdict

class LFUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.min_freq = 0
        self.key_value = {}
        self.key_freq = {}
        self.freq_keys = defaultdict(OrderedDict)                # frequency to an ordered set of keys, oldest first

    def _touch(self, key):
        freq = self.key_freq[key]
        del self.freq_keys[freq][key]                                # remove from its current frequency group
        if not self.freq_keys[freq] and freq == self.min_freq:
            self.min_freq += 1                                          # that group is now empty
        self.key_freq[key] = freq + 1
        self.freq_keys[freq + 1][key] = None                           # re-insert as most recent in the next group

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.key_value:
            return -1
        self._touch(key)
        return self.key_value[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.capacity == 0:
            return
        if key in self.key_value:
            self.key_value[key] = value
            self._touch(key)
            return
        if len(self.key_value) >= self.capacity:
            oldest_key, _ = self.freq_keys[self.min_freq].popitem(last=False)  # evict least recently used at minFreq
            del self.key_value[oldest_key]
            del self.key_freq[oldest_key]
        self.key_value[key] = value
        self.key_freq[key] = 1
        self.freq_keys[1][key] = None
        self.min_freq = 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cache = LFUCache(2)
    cache.put(1, 1)
    cache.put(2, 2)
    print(cache.get(1))
    cache.put(3, 3)
    print(cache.get(2))
    print(cache.get(3))
    cache.put(4, 4)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for every get and put operation, including eviction.
Space: O(capacity), for the value, frequency, and grouped key structures.
Why This Works

Grouping keys by frequency into buckets, combined with a minFreq pointer that only ever changes by exactly 1, up when its bucket empties, reset to 1 whenever a brand-new key is inserted, guarantees the minFreq bucket always holds exactly the currently lowest-frequency keys, with no comparison needed at read time. Within that bucket, keeping keys in insertion order, and always moving a key to the "most recent" end whenever it is used again, guarantees the oldest remaining entry is always the correct least-recently-used one to evict, resolving the tie-break exactly as required.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Structure","What it guarantees in O(1)"],"rows":[["The bucket at minFreq","The exact set of keys currently at the lowest frequency, ready for eviction from its oldest end"],["An insertion-ordered structure per bucket","Correct least-recently-used tie-breaking within any single frequency level"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Touching a key removes it from its current frequency's ordered group before incrementing its frequency, since a key's position must be fully cleared from the old bucket before it can correctly land in the new one.

The minFreq bump only happens when the just-vacated bucket was both the current minFreq bucket and now empty, since a key leaving a non-minimum bucket never affects where the true minimum currently sits.

Re-inserting a touched key always places it as the most recent entry of its new, frequency plus 1, group, correctly reflecting that it was just used, ahead of any key that has been sitting at that frequency longer.
put on a brand new key always resets minFreq to exactly 1, since a freshly inserted key starts at frequency 1, which by definition can never be beaten by anything already in the cache.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (full scan to find eviction candidate)","O(1) for get/put, O(capacity) for eviction","O(capacity)","Correct, but the required full scan for eviction violates the problem's strict O(1)-per-operation requirement"],["Optimized (frequency buckets, recency-ordered within each)","O(1) for every operation","O(capacity)","Both the frequency comparison and the recency tie-break are answered structurally, with no scanning"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

LFU Cache is a direct, specialized application of the same "bucket by a changing property, ordered by recency within each bucket" pattern used in All O`one Data Structure and Maximum Frequency Stack, here applied to frequency buckets that additionally need internal recency ordering for correct tie breaking.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to reset minFreq to 1 every time a brand new key is inserted, since a fresh key always starts at frequency 1, which is always the new minimum.
Only incrementing minFreq without checking whether the group that just lost its key is actually empty, which can incorrectly skip over frequency groups that still have other members.

Using a plain, unordered set per frequency bucket instead of an insertion-ordered structure, which would lose the ability to correctly identify the least recently used key within a tied frequency group.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Capacity 0","put should do nothing at all, and get should always return -1, since the cache can never hold any key"],["Updating an existing key's value via put","Must also count as a use and move that key up in frequency, not just overwrite its value silently, since put on an existing key is itself an access"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly connect this problem to the simpler LRU Cache first, frequency ignored, only recency matters, then explain that LFU adds one more dimension, frequency, requiring a hash map of ordered structures instead of just one.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Design a cache with an eviction rule that has a primary and a secondary tie-break criterion" points toward bucketing by the primary criterion, here frequency, and using a recency-ordered structure within each bucket for the secondary criterion, here LRU.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How does this compare to a plain LRU Cache? LRU Cache is a strict simplification of this exact structure: it only needs one recency-ordered structure overall, since frequency is ignored entirely, whereas LFU needs one such structure per frequency bucket, plus the minFreq pointer to know which bucket to evict from.

What if ties needed to be broken by most recently used instead of least? Simply evict from the opposite end of each frequency bucket's ordered structure, promoting to the same end used for insertion either way.

How would you handle a very large key space where most frequency buckets are usually empty? Only create a bucket's ordered structure lazily, the first time a key actually reaches that frequency, and delete it immediately once it becomes empty, exactly as the optimized solution already does, to avoid wasting memory on frequencies nothing currently occupies.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Direct specialization of All O`one Data Structure's frequency-bucket-linked-list pattern, adding a recency-ordered structure inside each bucket for the secondary tie-break.
Directly builds on the classic LRU Cache design, a hash map plus doubly linked list for O(1) recency tracking, reusing that exact recency mechanism once per frequency bucket instead of once globally.
Same "primary bucket, secondary order within bucket" two-level structuring seen whenever an eviction or ranking rule has more than one criterion to satisfy in order.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) for get and put in the common case, O(capacity) for eviction, O(capacity) space.
Optimized (frequency buckets with recency ordering): O(1) for every operation, O(capacity) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Frequency-bucketed hash map, each bucket an insertion-ordered structure for recency-based tie-breaking, plus a running minFreq pointer
Core Idea: Bucket keys by frequency for O(1) lowest-frequency access, and keep each bucket internally ordered by recency so the correct least-recently-used tie-break is also O(1)
Time: O(1) for get and put, including eviction
Space: O(capacity)

Most Important Observation: A two-level eviction rule, a primary criterion then a secondary tie-break, is solved by bucketing on the primary criterion and ordering within each bucket by the secondary one
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Bucket by frequency, LRU-order inside each bucket, minFreq resets to 1 on every fresh key
